title: Heraldry, Coats of Arms & Manorial Records

subChunks.title: Heraldry, Coats of Arms & Manorial Records

storyBeats.txt: No subject in family history generates more profitable confusion than heraldry, Theodora said drily. Every year, thousands of people spend money on 'family crests' that have no legal connection to their family whatsoever. And every year, genealogists spend time explaining why those purchases were worthless.

Arms belong to a specific individual and their legitimate descendants in the male line — not to a surname. The fact that your name is Hartley does not mean that the Hartley arms are yours. Someone called Hartley was granted those arms to that Hartley. Not to you.

That said, heraldry and the records of the College of Arms are genuinely valuable genealogical sources. The Heralds' Visitations recorded gentry pedigrees from the 1530s to the 1680s. Arms records can extend a documented line backwards centuries. You just need to know what they actually prove.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Walk into almost any heraldry shop online and you will be offered your 'family coat of arms' for a modest fee. The product will typically be a generic image of a shield associated with a common spelling of your surname. It will be historically meaningless. Arms are not granted to surnames; they are granted to individuals and their direct male-line descendants through a specific grant or descent.

This widespread misunderstanding obscures the genuine genealogical value of heraldry. The records of the College of Arms in London — the institution that has controlled the granting and recording of English arms since the 15th century — include the Heralds' Visitations, comprehensive gentry pedigrees recorded from the 1530s to the 1680s. Understanding what heraldry actually is, and how to use its records properly, transforms it from commercial mythology into a serious research tool.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is Heraldry?

Heraldry is a system of hereditary symbols displayed on shields, banners, and other surfaces, originally developed for identification on the battlefield in the 12th century. In England, the right to bear arms became regulated by the Crown through the College of Arms (incorporated 1484). Arms were granted by royal authority (through the College) to specific individuals and could be inherited by their legitimate male-line descendants.

Key heraldic terms: arms (the complete design on the shield); blazon (the precise verbal description of the arms in heraldic language); crest (a three-dimensional device worn on top of a helmet — not the whole arms, despite common misuse); achievement (the complete heraldic display including shield, crest, helm, mantling, supporters, and motto); quartering (dividing the shield to show the arms of inherited family lines through heiress marriages).

The College of Arms

The College of Arms (Heralds' College) in London is the official heraldic authority for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (Scotland has the Court of the Lord Lyon). It holds the official register of all arms granted since the 15th century, and the records of the Heralds' Visitations (c.1530–1686).

The College's records are not freely accessible online; researchers must write to the College or visit in person. For a fee, the College will check whether specific arms are recorded and whether a claimed connection to them can be verified. The College can also grant new arms to individuals who apply and are deemed eligible.

Heralds' Visitations as Genealogical Sources

Between the 1530s and the 1680s, the College of Arms conducted periodic Visitations of each county to record and verify gentry pedigrees and confirm or disallow arms claims. Heralds visited each county, interviewed heads of gentry families, and recorded their claimed descents — often going back several generations. Claims were signed by the head of the family.

Visitation records are invaluable for: extending documented lines into the 16th and 15th centuries; identifying collateral branches; confirming claimed relationships between families; and bridging the period between parish registers and earlier medieval records. Most have been published by county record societies (Harleian Society is the principal publisher) and are widely available in libraries and online (Internet Archive, HathiTrust).

Important caveat: Visitation pedigrees are claimed pedigrees, not verified ones. Many were accepted by the Heralds without documentary verification. Some are demonstrably incorrect. They should be treated as a starting point — a hypothesis to be tested against original records — not as authoritative proof of descent.

Manorial Records: The Genealogical Landscape

Manors were the basic unit of rural England from the Norman Conquest until the 20th century. Each manor was held by a lord from a superior lord (in a feudal chain ultimately reaching the Crown) and consisted of demesne lands (farmed directly for the lord) and tenant holdings. Tenants paid rent, performed services, and appeared before the manorial court.

Courts baron: Administered the copyhold tenure — the form of landholding in which a tenant held land 'by copy of the court roll' (i.e., their title was recorded in the court roll). Admission of a new tenant (by inheritance, purchase, or surrender) was recorded in the roll. Deaths of copyhold tenants triggered the heriot payment (best beast or equivalent). These records provide a chain of tenure for specific properties.

Courts leet: Exercised local criminal jurisdiction (petty offences, presentments, local administrative matters). Separate from the court baron in theory, though often combined in practice.

Finding surviving court rolls: Use the Manorial Documents Register (TNA, online) to identify holdings. Many have been transcribed and published by county record societies. Some are in private hands (estates, solicitors' offices); the MDR records these locations.

Manorial Records as Genealogical Evidence

A series of manorial court rolls provides: names of tenants at specific dates; relationships (son inheriting from father; widow inheriting from husband; nephew inheriting from uncle — the last demonstrates collateral kinship); approximate death dates (when the heriot appears or a successor is admitted); and addresses (specific copyhold fields, strips, or messuages).

A well-preserved manorial series can trace a family's property holding continuously from the 13th to the 19th century — far exceeding anything parish registers can provide for the pre-1538 period.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what 'coat of arms' actually means in English heraldry — and why you can't legally claim a coat of arms just because you share the same surname as someone who had one.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You find a published Heralds' Visitation for Yorkshire (1563/4) listing 'Robert Hartley of Pontefract' with a pedigree showing his father Thomas Hartley and grandfather John Hartley. Your documented post-1538 research has established a Robert Hartley of Pontefract baptised in 1538, whose father was a Thomas Hartley. How would you evaluate whether this Visitation pedigree might refer to your Robert Hartley, and what original records would you use to test the claimed descent?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The circumstantial match is promising: same name, same location, and the Visitation's Robert is consistent with a person born c.1538 appearing in a 1563/4 Visitation as an adult. However, Visitation pedigrees must be treated as hypotheses, not proofs.

Evaluation steps: (1) Check the Visitation pedigree for any documentary anchor — does it give dates, specific property descriptions, or other details that can be cross-referenced against original records? (2) If the Visitation claims Robert's father was Thomas, search manorial court records for Pontefract township for a Thomas Hartley making an admission of Robert (or Robert being admitted as heir to Thomas). (3) Search for Thomas Hartley in the 1543 or 1545 lay subsidy rolls for the West Riding if available. (4) Check the Pontefract area parish registers (if they survive from 1538) for baptisms of children of Thomas Hartley consistent with the Visitation's claimed siblings. (5) Search Pontefract area probate records for a will of Thomas Hartley naming a son Robert. (6) If John Hartley (grandfather) is claimed — search for him in the pre-1538 sources described in the previous lesson: manorial rolls, subsidy rolls.

Accept the Visitation connection only if at least two or three of these corroborating checks are positive and none contradicts the claimed relationship. State in any proof argument: 'Consistent with the Visitation entry for Robert Hartley of Pontefract (1563/4), subject to the following corroboration...'
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A client shows you a framed 'Family Coat of Arms' for the surname 'Fletcher' she bought online. She wants to know if it is legitimately hers. Explain: (1) how heraldic arms actually work in English law; (2) what the online purchase almost certainly represents; (3) what steps you would take to determine whether her documented Fletcher family has any legitimate connection to a grant of arms; and (4) what the College of Arms could do for her if she wanted to establish a genuine heraldic identity.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) In English heraldic law, arms are granted by the Earl Marshal through the College of Arms to a specific individual. The grant conveys the right to bear those arms and to pass them to legitimate male-line descendants. Arms belong to a person and their direct descendants, not to a surname. Two men called Fletcher may be entirely unrelated, and only one (or neither) has any legitimate claim to specific Fletcher arms.

(2) The online purchase almost certainly represents a generic design associated with the name Fletcher — possibly based on a real grant to someone called Fletcher at some historical point, but with no legal connection to your client's family unless she can document descent from the original grantee in the male line. This is a widely criticised commercial practice; it has no heraldic legal standing and the 'achievement' is effectively decorative merchandise.

(3) Steps: First, establish through genealogical research who the client's earliest documented Fletcher male-line ancestor was. Then write to the College of Arms requesting a search of their records for any grant of arms to a Fletcher family consistent with the geographic and temporal location of the client's line. The College will charge a search fee. If a grant is found, the client must then demonstrate documented male-line descent from the grantee — ideally through a proof argument meeting GPS standards.

(4) If no applicable grant is found, or if descent cannot be proven, the client can apply to the College of Arms for a new grant of arms in her own right (or her husband's, if she wishes a marital achievement). This is a formal process involving an application to a Herald, a grant fee, and the design of a unique achievement. The grant would then legitimately belong to her and her male-line descendants. This is the proper route to a genuine heraldic identity for someone who cannot establish descent from an existing grantee.
learningObjectives: Explain the legal basis of English heraldry and why arms belong to individuals and their male-line descendants, not to surnames.
Describe the Heralds' Visitations as genealogical sources and explain their evidential limitations.
Explain how manorial court rolls document tenant families, including what a copyhold admission, heriot, and succession record provide.
Describe the Manorial Documents Register and its role in locating surviving court roll series.
commonMistakes: Treating a commercially purchased 'family coat of arms' as having any legal heraldic standing.
Accepting Heralds' Visitation pedigrees as verified fact rather than as claimed lineages requiring corroboration.
Confusing 'crest' (the device on top of the helmet) with 'arms' (the complete heraldic achievement).
Failing to use the Manorial Documents Register before concluding that no court rolls survive for a given manor.
assessmentCriteria: Accurately explains the individual (not surname-based) nature of heraldic arms in English law.
Treats Visitation pedigrees as hypotheses requiring corroboration, not as independent proof of descent.
Correctly describes how manorial court records document succession, deaths, and family relationships.
Demonstrates knowledge of the College of Arms as a research resource and the MDR as a locator for surviving court rolls.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The official heraldic authority for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (incorporated 1484), holding records of all arms grants and the Heralds' Visitations; located in Queen Victoria Street, London.

Periodic surveys by College of Arms heralds (c.1530–1686) recording and verifying gentry pedigrees — published by the Harleian Society and available online; valuable but not authoritative without corroboration.
Form of manorial tenure in which a tenant held land 'by copy of the court roll'; admission, surrender, and succession were recorded in court rolls, creating a continuous property chain.
Death duty paid by a copyhold tenant's heir on succession — typically the best beast or a cash equivalent; its appearance in the court roll is indirect evidence of the previous tenant's death.
Scotland's heraldic authority, equivalent to the College of Arms; has jurisdiction over Scottish heraldry and maintains a separate Register of Arms.
Learned society publishing transcriptions of Heralds' Visitations and other heraldic and genealogical records since 1869; volumes available in libraries and on the Internet Archive.

questions.questionHtml: In English heraldic law, to whom do arms belong?
options: All persons who share the same surname
The oldest family of that surname in England
The specific individual to whom they were granted and their legitimate male-line descendants
Any person who has purchased a verified heraldic design
questions.correctAnswer: The specific individual to whom they were granted and their legitimate male-line descendants
questions.explanationHtml: Arms in English heraldry are granted to a specific individual by the Earl Marshal through the College of Arms. The right to bear those arms descends to legitimate male-line descendants of the grantee — not to all bearers of the same surname.

questions.questionHtml: A manorial court roll records: '14 October 1683: Thomas Whitfield admitted to one messuage and 10 acres in Nether Whitfield as son and heir of John Whitfield lately deceased; heriot paid one bay mare.' What genealogical information does this provide?
options: Direct evidence that Thomas Whitfield purchased land from John Whitfield
Evidence that John Whitfield died shortly before 14 October 1683, that Thomas was his son and heir, and that the family held specific copyhold land in Nether Whitfield
Evidence that John Whitfield had a horse and transferred it to Thomas as a gift
Indirect evidence only that someone named Whitfield lived in this area
questions.correctAnswer: Evidence that John Whitfield died shortly before 14 October 1683, that Thomas was his son and heir, and that the family held specific copyhold land in Nether Whitfield
questions.explanationHtml: The court roll entry provides: the approximate date of John's death (before the admission); direct evidence of the father-son relationship; evidence of the specific property held; and the heriot (best beast) paid. This is a rich genealogical record combining approximate death date and family relationship for a landowning family.

questions.questionHtml: A Heralds' Visitation for a county (1620) records a pedigree naming your ancestor's family going back to 1480. How should you treat this pedigree in your genealogical research?
options: Accept it as definitive proof of descent to 1480 — Heralds would not record inaccurate pedigrees
Ignore it entirely — Visitation records are unreliable and should not be used
Treat it as a hypothesis to be tested — a promising starting point requiring corroboration from independent original records before the claimed descent can be accepted
Use it only for the post-1538 section, which can be verified against parish registers
questions.correctAnswer: Treat it as a hypothesis to be tested — a promising starting point requiring corroboration from independent original records before the claimed descent can be accepted
questions.explanationHtml: Visitation pedigrees are claimed pedigrees recorded at one point in time, often without documentary verification by the Heralds. Many contain errors, embellishments, or claims that cannot be substantiated. They are a valuable starting point — not a proof — and must be tested against surviving original records (manorial rolls, probate, subsidy rolls) before being accepted.
